intro: Walk into almost any skatepark and you will hear it: the long, rough scrape of metal trucks on a steel-capped ledge, or the hiss of a deck sliding across a waxed rail. Grinds and slides began on the rounded coping of empty pools in the late 1970s. After skaters learned to ollie on flat ground in the early 1980s, they carried those tricks to curbs, ledges and rails everywhere.

This unit has two halves. The first teaches the tricks step by step, starting on a low painted curb or flat bar with a helmet, wrist guards and knee pads: the 50-50, the 5-0, the boardslide, the noseslide and the tailslide, plus how to approach, where to look and how to bail. The second half explains the physics underneath every grind: the friction force, the normal force, how fast a grind slows and how far it goes.

By the end, you will be able to explain each trick's steps with front foot and back foot, and use f = μN, a = μg and d = v²/(2μg) to predict how far a board will slide. You will also see why a little wax or a little more speed can make a grind go so much farther.
bigQuestion: How do skaters use balance, speed and friction to ride along an edge, and how can physics predict how far they will go?

title: Grinds and Slides

chapters.title: Grinds and Slides Step by Step
chapters.bigQuestion: How does a skater go from rolling past a curb to sliding along it with control?

story.title: The First Scrape
story.kicker: A skater waxes a painted curb and hears her trucks grind for the very first time.
paragraphs: Marisol kneels beside the low painted curb at the edge of the skatepark's flat area. The curb is about as tall as her shoe is long. She pulls a small block of skate wax from her pocket and rubs it along the top edge in short strokes. A thin, shiny film builds up on the yellow paint. She tests it with a fingertip. It feels slick, almost greasy.

She buckles her helmet and checks that it sits low on her forehead, two fingers above her eyebrows. Wrist guards, knee pads, flat shoes. For weeks she has practiced her ollie on the open concrete until she could pop it while rolling every time. Today she wants to put that ollie on top of the curb.

She pushes off slowly and rides beside the curb, close and almost parallel, the way her coach showed her. On the first three tries she only ollies up onto the curb top and rolls off again. Her coach nods and says that is exactly the right first step. On the fourth try she aims her board at the edge itself, keeps her knees bent and looks at the far end of the curb instead of at her feet.

Both trucks land on the corner of the curb. For a moment she hears a long, rough scrape, metal on painted concrete, and feels a buzz come up through her shoes. Then the board slows and tips off the side. She steps off with both feet, jogs a few steps and laughs. It lasted barely a meter, but it was a grind. She walks back to the start, rubs on a little more wax and lines up again.
story.think: Marisol practiced ollying onto the curb before she tried to grind it. Why might that smaller step help her feel ready?

lessons.title: Grinds, Slides and a Safe Start
lessons.mainIdea: A grind rides on the trucks and a slide rides on the deck, and both start on something low with your gear on.
reading: Skaters use two words for riding along an edge. In a *grind*, the metal trucks scrape along the edge. The axle and the hanger, the T-shaped metal part that holds the axle, take the contact. In a *slide*, the wooden underside of the deck rubs along the edge instead. Both tricks use a *ledge*, a long edge like a curb or a concrete block, or a *rail*, a metal bar or pipe.

Start low. A painted curb at a skatepark or a flat bar a few inches off the ground is the right first obstacle. A flat bar is a straight metal rail that sits level, close to the ground, on short legs. If you fall from a low curb, you only drop a short way. Stairs, handrails and tall ledges come much later, at a skatepark, when a skater has years of control.

Before you try, put on a helmet that fits snugly and is buckled, plus wrist guards and knee pads. Wear flat-soled shoes that grip the grip tape. Pick a dry, smooth place away from cars and away from people walking. Most grinds and slides need a steady ollie while rolling, so practice that first. If your ollie gets you a few inches off flat ground every time, you are ready to begin.

a trick in which the wooden underside of the deck rubs along an edge or rail
a long, raised edge such as a curb or concrete block that skaters grind or slide on
a metal bar or pipe that skaters grind or slide on

lessons.title: Wax on the Edge
lessons.mainIdea: Skate wax makes an edge slicker so the board slides farther, and a thin coat is enough.
reading: New concrete and fresh paint can grab a board and stop it short. Skaters fix this with *wax*. Skate wax comes in small blocks sold for skating. Some skaters use plain paraffin, the kind of wax used in candles. Rub the block along the top corner of the ledge in short strokes, then rub it in with the side of the block until the edge looks shiny.

A thin coat works best. Too little and the trucks still catch. Too much and the edge gets so slick the board can shoot out from under you, or it builds up in sticky lumps. Try one run, then add a little more if the board stops short. Wax wears off as people skate, so a ledge may need a fresh coat after a session.

Wax only edges where skating is allowed, like the curbs and ledges at a skatepark. Wax leaves marks and can make a public step slippery for people walking. A good habit is to bring your own small block, wax just the edge you are using, and leave the area as clean as you found it. Wax also works on a flat bar, though metal rails are already smoother than concrete.

words.d: a slippery coating rubbed on an edge so a board slides along it more easily
a plain, colorless wax, like candle wax, that some skaters use on edges
a stretch of time spent skating one spot or practicing one trick

look.title: Two Strokes of Wax
look.text: Picture two halves of the same curb. The left half has no wax. When a board grinds it, the trucks scrape loudly and stop after a short way. The right half has a thin, shiny coat rubbed in. The same grind at the same speed hisses along and keeps going about twice as far.
look.prompt: If a board shot out from under a skater on a waxed curb, what might have gone wrong with the wax?

check.q: Why do skaters put wax on a ledge?
choices: to make the edge rougher so the board stops
to make the edge slicker so the board slides farther
to paint the edge a new color
check.why: Wax makes the edge slick, so trucks and decks slide farther.

check.q: What can happen if a skater puts on far too much wax?
choices: the board can shoot out or the wax builds into sticky lumps
check.why: Too much wax makes the edge overly slick or lumpy, so a thin coat is better.

check.q: Where is it right to wax an edge?
choices: only where skating is allowed, like a skatepark ledge
check.why: Wax leaves marks and makes steps slippery, so wax only where skating is allowed.

lessons.title: Practice Without Rolling
lessons.mainIdea: Setting the board on the edge while standing still lets you feel the balance point before you add speed.
reading: Before rolling, learn what a grind feels like with the board still. Set your board on the curb so both trucks sit on the top corner and the wheels hang over the side you will ride from. Hold a friend's shoulder or a fence. Step your back foot over the back bolts, then your front foot over the front bolts. The bolts are the screw heads that hold the trucks to the deck.

Now feel where your weight must go. Lean too far toward the ground side and the board tips off. Lean toward the top of the curb and the wheels drop onto it. Somewhere in the middle, with your knees bent and your shoulders level, the board balances on the edge. That middle spot is the feeling you are hunting for when you are moving.

Next, try a rolling drill that is not a grind at all. Ride slowly next to the curb, almost parallel, and ollie up onto the flat top of the curb. Roll along the top and off the end. This teaches you to judge the distance and the timing. When that feels easy ten times in a row, start aiming a little lower, so your trucks meet the edge itself.

words.d: the screw heads on top of the deck that hold the trucks on; skaters place their feet over them
the spot where your weight sits so the board stays on the edge without tipping either way
a small practice move repeated to build one part of a skill

look.title: Standing on the Edge
look.text: Picture the board resting along the corner of a curb with no wheels touching the ground. Both trucks sit on the corner. Your back foot is over the back bolts and your front foot is over the front bolts. A friend's shoulder steadies you. You shift your hips an inch toward the ground side and feel the board start to tip. You shift back and it settles.
look.prompt: Try this with the board still. Which way did the board tip first when your weight moved?

check.q: In the standing drill, where do both trucks rest?
choices: on the top corner of the curb
on top of the grip tape
check.why: The drill sets both trucks on the edge so you can feel the grind's balance.

check.q: Where should your front foot go in the standing drill?
choices: on the very tip of the tail
check.why: The reading places the front foot over the front bolts and the back foot over the back bolts.

check.q: Which rolling drill comes before aiming at the edge itself?
choices: jump down a set of stairs
ride the curb at top speed
ollie onto the flat top of the curb and roll off the end
check.why: Ollying onto the curb top teaches distance and timing before you aim at the edge.

lessons.title: The 50-50
lessons.mainIdea: In a 50-50, both trucks grind the edge at once with your weight centered between them.
reading: The *50-50* is the first grind most skaters learn. Both trucks grind the edge at the same time, so the weight is shared fifty-fifty. It came from pool skating in the late 1970s, when skaters ground the coping, the rounded edge at the top of a pool wall. On flat ground it is done on curbs, ledges and flat bars.

Here are the steps. First, roll toward the curb at a slow, steady speed, nearly parallel to it, with your feet in ollie position: back foot on the tail, front foot just behind the front bolts. Next, when your front wheels are close to the edge, ollie up and a little toward it. Then guide the board so both trucks land on the corner at once. Bend your knees as they land and keep your weight centered between the trucks.

Ride the edge with your shoulders lined up with the curb. At the end, let the board roll off the end and land with bent knees, rolling away. A common problem is landing with only the back truck on, which tips the nose down onto the top. The fix is to ollie a little higher and level the board in the air. Another is landing too far onto the top. Then come in closer to the edge before you pop.

words.d: a grind with both trucks on the edge at the same time, weight shared evenly
the rounded metal or concrete edge at the top of a ramp or pool wall
back foot on the tail and front foot just behind the front bolts, ready to pop

look.title: A 50-50, Step by Step
look.text: Step 1: Roll slowly beside the curb, almost parallel. Step 2: Feet in ollie position, knees bent. Step 3: Pop the tail with the back foot and slide the front foot up. Step 4: Level the board in the air and steer it toward the edge. Step 5: Both trucks land on the corner. Step 6: Knees stay bent, eyes on the far end. Step 7: Roll off the end and ride away.
look.prompt: Which step would you practice again if only your back truck landed on the edge?

check.q: What touches the edge in a 50-50?
check.why: In a 50-50 both trucks grind at once, sharing the weight evenly.

check.q: Where did skaters first grind coping in the late 1970s?
choices: on the rounded edges of pools
check.why: The 50-50 grew from pool skating, grinding the coping at the top of the wall.

check.q: Only your back truck keeps landing on the edge. What is the fix from the reading?
choices: ollie a little higher and level the board in the air
push much faster at the curb
look down at your front foot
check.why: Leveling the board in the air lets both trucks land at once.

lessons.title: The 5-0
lessons.mainIdea: A 5-0 grinds on the back truck only, balanced like a manual with the nose up.
reading: In a *5-0* (say five-oh), only the back truck grinds. The nose stays up in the air and the front truck hangs above the edge. If you have practiced a *manual*, balancing on the back wheels while rolling on flat ground, you already know the feeling. A 5-0 is a manual done on an edge instead of on the ground.

The steps begin like a 50-50. Roll toward the curb nearly parallel at a slow, steady speed. Ollie up toward the edge, but keep a little more weight on the back foot as you land, so the back truck meets the corner first and the nose stays up. Your back foot sits over the back bolts, not on the very end of the tail. Your front foot stays light over the front bolts, steering the nose level.

The hard part is the balance. If you lean too far back, the tail drags on the curb and the board stops. If you lean too far forward, the front truck drops and the trick turns into a 50-50. Aim to keep the nose a few inches up and steady. At the end, press the front foot down a little as the board rolls off, so both trucks come down together on the ground.

words.d: a grind on the back truck only, with the nose held up in the air
balancing on the back wheels while rolling, with the nose up off the ground
when the tail scrapes the surface because too much weight is on the back foot

look.title: Manual, Then 5-0
look.text: Picture two skaters. One rolls across flat ground with the nose a few inches up, balanced over the back wheels. The other rolls along a curb with the nose a few inches up, balanced over the back truck as it scrapes the edge. Their bodies look almost the same: knees bent, arms out, eyes ahead.
look.prompt: How long can you hold a manual on flat ground? Why might a longer manual help your 5-0?

check.q: Which part grinds in a 5-0?
check.why: A 5-0 is a grind on the back truck with the nose up.

check.q: In a 5-0, the tail drags and the board stops. What happened?
choices: the skater leaned too far back
the skater leaned too far forward
the front truck was too loose
check.why: Too much weight on the back foot drops the tail onto the edge, which stops the board.

check.q: Which flat-ground trick feels most like a 5-0?
check.why: A manual balances on the back wheels with the nose up, the same balance as a 5-0.

lessons.title: Angle and Speed
lessons.mainIdea: Come in at a shallow angle and a steady, comfortable speed so the trucks lock on and carry to the end.
reading: The *approach* is the path you ride toward the obstacle. For a 50-50 or 5-0, come in at a shallow angle, nearly parallel to the edge, but slightly toward it. A good picture is a door opened only a little. If you ride straight at the curb, the board will hit the edge and stop, or fly over the top. If you ride exactly parallel and far away, you cannot reach the edge when you pop.

Speed matters as much as angle. A friction force slows the board the whole time it grinds, so a board that arrives slowly stops partway. A board that arrives too fast is hard to steer onto the edge and hard to control at the end. Start at an easy rolling speed, a little faster than a brisk walk, and add a little speed on each try once you can land on the edge.

You can also choose a side. In a *frontside* grind your chest and toes face the edge as you approach. In a *backside* grind your back and heels face it. Both are normal, and each skater may feel more comfortable on one side first. Pick one side, practice it until it feels steady, then learn the other.

words.d: the path and speed a skater uses riding toward an obstacle
how fast the board is moving, measured in meters per second
a grind done with your chest and toes facing the edge as you approach
a grind done with your back and heels facing the edge as you approach

look.title: Example Approach Speeds
look.cite: Example speeds for comparison; real speeds vary with the skater and the surface
look.prompt: Which example speed matches the easy roll the reading suggests for a first grind?

check.q: What happens if you ride straight at the curb instead of at a shallow angle?
choices: the board hits the edge and stops, or flies over
check.why: A steep approach slams the board into the edge or carries it over the top.

check.q: Why does a board that arrives too slowly stop partway?
choices: friction slows it the whole time it grinds
check.why: Friction acts during the whole grind, so a slow board runs out of speed early.

check.q: In a frontside grind, what faces the edge as you approach?
check.why: Frontside means you approach with your chest and toes toward the edge.

lessons.title: The Boardslide
lessons.mainIdea: In a boardslide the board turns across the rail and the middle of the deck slides along it, between the trucks.
reading: In a *boardslide*, the board sits across the rail, crosswise, with the rail between the two trucks. The middle of the deck's underside slides along the metal. A low flat bar is the classic place to learn it, because the bar is narrow and slick. The board points across the bar while you slide along it.

Here are the steps. First, roll toward the flat bar nearly straight on, but just to one side of its end. Next, ollie and turn your shoulders and the board a quarter turn, so the board crosses over the bar. Then land with the bar under the middle of the deck, between your feet. Keep your knees bent and your weight right over the bar, with your head above it.

To come off, turn your shoulders back a quarter turn at the end of the bar, so the board points forward again, and roll away. A common problem is leaning away from the direction you are sliding. Your feet then shoot forward and you sit down. The fix is to keep your weight over the bar and your eyes on its end. Another is landing with a truck on the bar, which hangs up the board; ollie a little higher to clear it.

words.d: a slide with the board crosswise on a rail so the middle of the deck slides between the trucks
a straight metal rail set level and low on short legs, used for learning grinds and slides
when a truck or wheel catches on an obstacle and stops the board suddenly

look.title: From Above
look.text: Picture looking down from above a low flat bar. The skater rolls toward its end, pops and turns. Now the board forms a plus sign with the bar: board across, bar along. The bar sits under the middle of the deck, between the front and back trucks. The skater slides along the bar, then turns the board back in line and rolls away.
look.prompt: Draw the plus sign the board and bar make. Where are the two trucks in your drawing?

check.q: Which part of the board touches the rail in a boardslide?
choices: the middle of the deck, between the trucks
check.why: A boardslide has the rail under the middle of the deck.

check.q: How is the board turned compared to the rail in a boardslide?
check.why: The board turns a quarter turn so it crosses the rail.

check.q: What usually happens if you lean away from the slide's direction?
choices: your feet shoot forward and you sit down
check.why: Leaning away lets the board run out from under your feet.

lessons.title: The Noseslide
lessons.mainIdea: In a noseslide, the board turns a quarter turn and only the nose slides on the ledge.
reading: The *nose* is the front end of the deck, past the front truck. In a *noseslide*, you ollie up, turn the board a quarter turn, and set only the underside of the nose on the ledge. The rest of the board hangs off the ground side, and the back wheels stay in the air. A waxed ledge works better than a round rail for learning it, because the nose sits flat on top.

Here are the steps. First, roll toward the ledge nearly parallel at an easy speed. Next, pop an ollie and turn your shoulders and the board a quarter turn toward the ledge. Then press your front foot onto the nose so the nose lands on the top edge. Most of your weight should sit over the front foot. Keep your back foot light on the tail and your knees bent.

To come off, push lightly with the front foot and turn your shoulders back a quarter turn, so the board lines up with your path and rolls away. A common problem is not getting enough weight on the nose. The board then slips off right away. The fix is to lean forward over the front foot and look toward the end of the ledge. Another is turning too far, past a quarter turn, so you come off pointing the wrong way.

words.d: the front end of the deck, past the front truck
a slide with the board turned a quarter turn so only the nose rests on the ledge
a turn of about 90 degrees, so the board points across your path

look.title: Weight on the Front
look.text: Picture a skater in a noseslide on a low waxed ledge. The board points away from the ledge, crosswise to the path. Only the nose rests on the top edge. The front knee is bent deep and the front shoulder leans out over the nose. The back foot rests lightly on the tail, which floats in the air over the ground.
look.prompt: Stand on a board on carpet and shift most of your weight to your front foot. How does it change your balance?

check.q: Which part of the board rests on the ledge in a noseslide?
check.why: A noseslide sets only the underside of the nose on the ledge.

check.q: Where should most of your weight be during a noseslide?
check.why: The nose carries the slide, so most weight goes over the front foot.

check.q: In a noseslide, the board slips off right away. What is the likely cause?
choices: not enough weight on the nose
too much wax on the wheels
a helmet that is too loose
check.why: Without enough weight on the nose, it will not stay on the ledge.

lessons.title: The Tailslide
lessons.mainIdea: A tailslide sets the tail on the ledge with the board turned a quarter turn and the weight over the back foot.
reading: The *tail* is the back end of the deck, past the back truck, the part you pop for an ollie. A *tailslide* is the back-end partner of the noseslide. You ollie, turn the board a quarter turn, and set the underside of the tail on the top edge of the ledge. The front of the board points out over the ground and the front wheels hang in the air.

Here are the steps. First, ride toward the ledge nearly parallel at an easy, steady speed. Next, ollie a little higher than usual, because the tail must reach the top of the ledge. Then turn your shoulders and the board a quarter turn and press the tail down onto the edge with your back foot. Keep most of your weight over the back foot, with your front foot steadying the board over the front bolts.

To come off, turn your shoulders back a quarter turn and let the board drop to the ground pointing forward, with knees bent. A common problem is the tail landing below the top of the ledge, against its side. The board then stops hard. The fix is to pop higher and keep the front knee bent so the board levels out. Many skaters find the tailslide harder than the noseslide, because the slide happens behind them, where they cannot see it as easily.

words.d: the back end of the deck, past the back truck, which you pop for an ollie
a slide with the board turned a quarter turn so only the tail rests on the ledge
the quick snap of the tail against the ground that lifts the board into an ollie

look.title: Nose or Tail?
look.text: Picture two skaters side by side on the same ledge. Both boards are turned a quarter turn. The first skater leans forward and the nose rests on the edge; the tail floats over the ground. The second leans back and the tail rests on the edge; the nose floats over the ground. Same ledge, opposite ends, opposite weight.
look.prompt: Name each trick. Which foot carries most of the weight in each one?

check.q: Which part rests on the ledge in a tailslide?
check.why: A tailslide sets the underside of the tail on the ledge.

check.q: Which foot carries most of the weight in a tailslide?
check.why: The tail is under the back foot, so most weight goes there.

check.q: Why does a tailslide often need a slightly higher ollie?
choices: the nose must touch the ground
the tail must reach the top of the ledge
check.why: If the pop is low, the tail hits the side of the ledge instead of the top.

lessons.title: Look Where You Want to Go
lessons.mainIdea: Keeping your eyes on the end of the ledge keeps your shoulders, hips and weight lined up for the whole grind.
reading: Your body tends to follow your eyes. If you stare down at your front foot during a grind, your head drops and your shoulders tip forward. That moves your weight off the balance point, and the board slides off early. Coaches tell skaters to look at the end of the ledge or rail instead, the spot where they plan to roll off.

Looking ahead also lines up your *shoulders*. For a 50-50 or 5-0, your shoulders should point along the ledge, the same direction as your path. For a boardslide, noseslide or tailslide, your shoulders turn with the board for the slide, then turn back for the exit. Your head and eyes lead the turn, and your shoulders and hips follow.

The *exit* is how you leave the obstacle. On a low curb, the simplest exit is rolling off the end and landing with bent knees, both feet over the bolts. Plan your exit before you start the trick, and look at that spot from the very beginning. A skater who knows where the trick ends rides it with more confidence than one who is only thinking about getting on.

words.d: the upper body's line, which skaters point along the path to keep the board on course
the way a skater leaves an obstacle at the end of a grind or slide
keeping your weight over the part of the board that is holding you up

look.title: Two Sets of Eyes
look.text: Picture two skaters in a 50-50 on the same curb. The first stares at her front foot. Her chin drops, her shoulders round forward, and her board slides off the ground side after half a meter. The second looks at the end of the curb. Her chin is up, her shoulders point along the curb, and she rides to the end and rolls away.
look.prompt: On your next roll on flat ground, pick a spot ahead and keep your eyes on it. Does your board go where you look?

check.q: Where should your eyes be during a grind?
choices: on the end of the ledge
check.why: Looking at the end keeps the head up and the weight on the balance point.

check.q: In a 50-50, which way should your shoulders point?
choices: along the ledge, the way you are going
check.why: For truck grinds, the shoulders line up with the ledge and your path.

check.q: When should you plan your exit?
check.why: Planning the exit first lets you look at it and ride the trick with confidence.

lessons.title: Bailing Safely
lessons.mainIdea: A good bail means stepping off and running it out when you can, and falling low and rolling when you cannot.
reading: To *bail* is to leave the board on purpose when a trick goes wrong. Every skater bails many times while learning a grind. The safest bail is a step-off: as soon as the board stops or tips, step both feet onto the ground on the side away from the obstacle and jog a few steps. The board may roll away, so check that no one is in its path.

Sometimes there is no time to step off. Then fall small. Bend your knees and get low, so you drop a short distance. Tuck your chin. Let your body roll onto the meaty side of your shoulder, your hip or your back instead of stopping all at once. Slide on your knee pads if you fall forward. Do not throw out locked, straight arms to catch yourself. Wrist injuries are among the most common skateboarding injuries, and wrist guards help prevent them.

Fear is a normal signal, not a weakness. If a trick scares you, make it smaller. Go back to the standing drill, lower the speed, or practice ollying onto the curb top again. A short practice session with many small, controlled tries builds a grind faster than a few big, scary ones. Stop when you are tired, because tired legs land badly.

words.d: to leave the board on purpose when a trick is going wrong
a bail where you put both feet on the ground and jog away from the board
to crouch low, tuck and roll so a fall is short and spread out

look.title: Who Should Ride
look.text: The American Academy of Pediatrics advises that children younger than 5 should not ride skateboards, and that children from 6 to 10 should skate only with an adult watching over them.
look.cite: American Academy of Pediatrics, guidance on skateboard safety
look.prompt: Why might a group of doctors give guidance by age? What could a grown-up do while a young skater practices grinds?

check.q: What is the safest bail when the board stops on a curb?
choices: step both feet off and jog a few steps
lock your arms straight and catch yourself
stay on and lean back hard
jump as high as you can
check.why: A step-off puts you on your feet with no fall at all.

check.q: Why should you not catch a fall with locked, straight arms?
choices: wrist injuries are among the most common, and locked arms take the whole hit
it makes the board roll faster
check.why: Locked arms put all the force into the wrists, a very common injury.

check.q: A trick feels scary. What does the reading suggest?
choices: make it smaller with a drill or less speed
check.why: Breaking a trick into smaller steps is how fear becomes progress.

lessons.title: A Step-by-Step Practice Plan
lessons.mainIdea: Grinds and slides come in a sensible order, each one building on the skills of the one before.
reading: Grinds and slides build on each other, so the order you learn them matters. A common path starts with a steady rolling ollie, then ollying onto the curb top, then the 50-50. The 50-50 teaches you to land on an edge with your weight centered. Next comes the 5-0, which adds the manual's balance on the back truck.

Slides usually come after you are comfortable on your trucks. A boardslide on a low flat bar teaches the quarter turn on and off. The noseslide and tailslide add turning plus putting most of your weight over one end. Each new trick reuses a skill you already have: the ollie, the quarter turn, a manual's balance, or looking at the end of the obstacle.

Keep each practice short and focused. Choose one trick and one side, frontside or backside, for a session. Warm up with ollies on flat ground. Count your clean tries instead of your falls. When one trick works on a low curb most of the time, it is ready for a slightly longer or slightly higher ledge at the skatepark, one small change at a time.

words.d: learning skills in an order where each step builds on the one before
easy skating at the start of a session that gets your body ready
an attempt where you land the trick and ride away in control

look.title: One Path Through the Tricks

Step 5: 5-0 on a low curb. Step 6: Boardslide on a low flat bar. Step 7: Noseslide on a waxed ledge. Step 8: Tailslide on a waxed ledge.

chapters.title: The Science of Friction on a Rail
chapters.bigQuestion: What decides how far a board slides along a ledge before friction stops it?

story.title: Same Speed, Twice as Far
story.kicker: Two skaters hit the same ledge at the same speed, and one slides twice as far.
paragraphs: Deshawn and Ana take turns on a long, low concrete ledge at their neighborhood skatepark. They have both learned the 50-50. They want to know who can grind farther. A friend stands beside the ledge with a tape measure and a phone timer.

To make it fair, they mark a starting line on the ground with chalk and push the same number of times. The friend times each skater over the last two meters before the ledge. Both arrive at about 3 meters per second, a little faster than a jog. Deshawn grinds first and comes off after a little over a meter. Ana grinds the next section of the same ledge and slides about twice as far.

At first they argue about technique. Then Ana points at the edge. Her half of the ledge is shiny with wax. Deshawn's half is bare, rough concrete where the paint has worn away. They switch halves and try again. This time Deshawn goes twice as far, and Ana stops short.

Nothing about the skaters changed. Their speed was the same and their weight hardly mattered. What changed was the surface, and with it the friction between the trucks and the edge. The measuring tape showed a pattern a physicist would recognize: cut the friction in half, and the slide distance doubles.
story.think: The skaters switched halves of the ledge and the results switched too. What does that test tell you about the cause?

lessons.title: What Friction Does
lessons.mainIdea: Friction is a force between two touching surfaces that pushes against the sliding, so it slows a grind.
reading: When metal trucks scrape along a concrete edge, they slow down. The force doing this is *friction*, a force between two surfaces that are touching. Friction always points against the sliding. If the board slides forward along the ledge, friction on the trucks points backward. That backward push is what eventually stops every grind and slide.

Physicists split friction into two kinds. Static friction holds two surfaces still against each other, like the grip between your shoe and the grip tape. Kinetic friction acts while two surfaces slide past each other, like the trucks on a ledge. For most pairs of surfaces, kinetic friction is a bit weaker than the most static friction can give. That is why a stuck board is harder to start sliding than to keep sliding.

Friction comes from the surfaces themselves. Up close, even a smooth rail has tiny bumps and pits. As the truck slides, those bumps catch, scrape and break, and the surfaces briefly stick together. A rough surface catches more. A slick coating, like wax, fills the pits and lets the surfaces slip. Isaac Newton's first law explains the rest: the board would keep moving if no force pushed against it.

words.d: a force between two touching surfaces that pushes against their sliding
friction that holds two surfaces still against each other
friction that acts while two surfaces slide past each other

look.title: Newton's First Law
look.text: Every body keeps on in its state of rest, or of moving at a steady speed in a straight line, unless forces acting on it make it change that state.
look.cite: Isaac Newton, Principia (1687), Law I; paraphrased from Andrew Motte's English translation (1729)
look.prompt: Use Newton's first law to explain why a grinding board slows down instead of sliding forever.

check.q: Which way does friction push on a board sliding forward along a ledge?
check.why: Friction always points against the direction of sliding.

check.q: Which kind of friction acts on trucks grinding a ledge?
check.why: Kinetic friction acts while surfaces slide past each other.

check.q: Why does wax lower friction?
choices: it fills tiny pits so surfaces slip past each other
it adds bumps to the rail
check.why: Wax smooths the tiny bumps and pits that catch and scrape.

lessons.title: The Normal Force
lessons.mainIdea: The normal force is the edge pushing up on the board; on a level ledge it equals the skater's weight.
reading: When you stand on a board on a ledge, gravity pulls you down. The ledge pushes back up. That upward push is called the *normal force*. Normal here means at a right angle, because the force points straight out of the surface. On a level ledge, with the skater not bouncing, the normal force exactly balances the weight.

Weight is the pull of gravity on a mass. It equals mass times g, where g is 9.8 meters per second squared near Earth's surface. Weight is a force, so it is measured in newtons, written N. One newton is about the weight of a small apple. Mass is measured in kilograms and stays the same anywhere; weight would change on the Moon.

Here is a worked example. A skater and board together have a mass of 60 kilograms. Weight = m times g = 60 kg times 9.8 m/s squared = 588 N. On a level ledge, the normal force is also 588 N. If the skater pushes down hard or lands from an ollie, the normal force jumps above 588 N for a moment, and so does the friction.

words.d: the push of a surface on an object, at a right angle to the surface
the pull of gravity on a mass; weight = mass times g
the SI unit of force, written N; about the weight of a small apple
how much matter an object has, measured in kilograms

look.title: Weight of Skater Plus Board
look.prompt: Check one row yourself. What is 75 times 9.8?

check.q: On a level ledge, what does the normal force equal?
choices: the weight of the skater and board
check.why: On a level surface the upward normal force balances the weight.

check.q: A skater and board have a mass of 50 kg. What is their weight?
check.why: Weight = 50 kg times 9.8 m/s squared = 490 N.

check.q: In what unit is weight measured?
check.why: Weight is a force, and force is measured in newtons.

lessons.title: Friction Equals Mu Times N
lessons.mainIdea: Kinetic friction force equals the coefficient of friction times the normal force: f = μN.
reading: Experiments show a simple pattern for sliding friction. Press two surfaces together twice as hard and the friction roughly doubles. Scientists write this as f = μN. Here f is the friction force, N is the normal force, and μ, the Greek letter mu, is the *coefficient of friction*. The coefficient is a plain number with no unit. It describes how grabby a pair of surfaces is.

The coefficient belongs to a pair of surfaces, not to one. Steel trucks on waxed steel have one value. The same trucks on rough concrete have a larger one. For example, a waxed metal rail might be around 0.2 and bare rough concrete around 0.5. These are example numbers, not fixed constants; real values change with wax, dirt, heat and wear.

Here is a worked example. The 60 kg skater from before grinds a ledge with an example coefficient μ = 0.30. The normal force is 588 N. Friction f = μN = 0.30 times 588 N = 176.4 N, about 176 N. That backward push is a little less than a third of the skater's weight. Notice that the size of the trucks' contact patch does not appear in the formula. For many surfaces, friction depends on the push, not on the area touching.

words.d: a number with no unit, written μ, that tells how strongly two surfaces resist sliding
the rule that kinetic friction force equals the coefficient of friction times the normal force
the small area where two surfaces actually touch

look.title: Amontons and the Load
look.text: Friction between sliding surfaces grows in proportion to the load pressing them together, and it does not depend on how large the touching area appears to be.
look.cite: Guillaume Amontons, report to the French Royal Academy of Sciences, 1699
look.prompt: How does Amontons's finding match the formula f = μN?

check.q: In f = μN, what does N stand for?
check.why: N is the normal force, the surface's push on the board.

check.q: With N = 600 N and μ = 0.25, what is the friction force?
Why is μ = 0.2 for a waxed rail only an example?
choices: real values change with wax, dirt, heat and wear
μ depends on the skater's age
check.why: The coefficient depends on the actual surfaces, so it is a typical value, not a constant.

lessons.title: Slowing Equals Mu Times g
lessons.mainIdea: On a level rail, a grinding board slows at a = μg, so the skater's mass cancels out.
reading: Newton's second law says force equals mass times acceleration, F = ma. Acceleration is how fast speed changes, in meters per second, each second. When friction is the only push along the ledge, it causes a *deceleration*, a slowing down. Divide the friction force by the mass and you get how quickly the board loses speed.

Put the pieces together. Friction f = μN, and on a level ledge N = mg. So f = μmg. The slowing is a = f divided by m = μmg divided by m. The m on top and the m on the bottom cancel, leaving a = μg. A heavier skater pushes harder on the ledge and gets more friction, but also has more mass to slow down. The two effects cancel exactly.

Here is a worked example. With μ = 0.30, the slowing is a = 0.30 times 9.8 m/s squared = 2.94 m/s squared. Each second, the board loses about 2.94 meters per second of speed. A board that starts the grind at 3.0 m/s stops after t = 3.0 divided by 2.94, about 1.0 second. That matches what skaters see: a grind on a bare ledge lasts about a second unless they bring more speed.

words.d: how fast speed changes, measured in meters per second, each second (m/s squared)
acceleration that slows an object down
Newton's second law: net force equals mass times acceleration

look.title: Light Skater, Heavy Skater
look.text: Picture two skaters on the same waxed ledge, both arriving at 3 m/s. One has a mass of 40 kg with the board, the other 80 kg. The heavier skater presses down twice as hard, so friction on the trucks is twice as big. But the heavier skater also has twice the mass to slow. Both slow at the same rate and stop at about the same spot.
look.prompt: Explain in your own words why mass cancels out in a = μg.

check.q: On a level ledge, what does the slowing of a grind equal?
check.why: a = μmg divided by m = μg, so mass cancels.

check.q: With μ = 0.20, what is the slowing?
check.why: a = 0.20 times 9.8 = 1.96 m/s squared.

check.q: Why do a light and a heavy skater slow at the same rate on the same ledge?
choices: light skaters push the ledge harder
more weight means more friction, but also more mass to slow
gravity is weaker for heavy skaters
check.why: Friction and mass both double together, so the slowing stays the same.

lessons.title: How Far a Grind Goes
lessons.mainIdea: A grind that starts at speed v slides a distance d = v² divided by (2μg) before it stops.
reading: If you know how fast the board starts and how quickly it slows, you can find how far it goes. For steady slowing from speed v down to zero, the *slide distance* is d = v squared divided by 2a. On a level ledge, a = μg, so d = v squared divided by (2μg). Here v is the speed in meters per second as the grind starts.

Here is a worked example, step by step. A skater starts a 50-50 at v = 3.0 m/s on a ledge with an example μ = 0.30. First, square the speed: 3.0 times 3.0 = 9.0. Next, find the bottom: 2 times 0.30 times 9.8 = 5.88. Then divide: d = 9.0 divided by 5.88 = 1.53 meters. The board grinds about one and a half meters before friction stops it.

The formula also works backward. Suppose you want to grind a ledge 2.0 m long with an example μ = 0.25. Solve for v: v squared = 2 times μ times g times d = 2 times 0.25 times 9.8 times 2.0 = 9.8. So v = the square root of 9.8, about 3.1 m/s. Arrive slower than that and the board stops before the end.

words.d: how far a board travels along an edge before friction stops it
the slide distance on a level edge for starting speed v and coefficient μ
to multiply a number by itself; 3 squared is 9

look.title: Working It Out
look.text: Starting speed v = 3.0 m/s. Coefficient μ = 0.30 (an example). Step 1: v squared = 9.0. Step 2: 2 times μ times g = 2 times 0.30 times 9.8 = 5.88. Step 3: d = 9.0 divided by 5.88 = 1.53 m. The trucks stop about a meter and a half down the ledge.
look.prompt: Redo the steps with v = 2.0 m/s. How far does the board go?

check.q: Which formula gives the slide distance on a level ledge?
check.why: The slide distance is v squared divided by 2μg.

check.q: A board starts at 2.0 m/s with μ = 0.20. How far does it slide? (2 times 0.20 times 9.8 = 3.92)
check.why: d = 4.0 divided by 3.92 = about 1.02 m.

check.q: What is the first step in the worked example?
check.why: The worked example starts by squaring v: 3.0 times 3.0 = 9.0.

lessons.title: Why Speed Carries a Grind
lessons.mainIdea: Slide distance grows with the square of speed, so doubling your speed makes a grind go four times as far.
reading: Look at the formula again: d = v squared divided by (2μg). The speed is squared. That means distance does not grow in step with speed. It grows much faster. Double the speed and the distance becomes 2 times 2 = 4 times as long. Triple the speed and it becomes 3 times 3 = 9 times as long.

Here is a worked example with μ = 0.30, so 2μg = 5.88. At 1.0 m/s, d = 1.0 divided by 5.88 = 0.17 m. At 2.0 m/s, d = 4.0 divided by 5.88 = 0.68 m. At 4.0 m/s, d = 16 divided by 5.88 = 2.72 m. Going from 2 to 4 m/s, the speed doubled and the distance went from 0.68 m to 2.72 m, four times as far.

This is why skaters say speed is your friend on a long ledge, and why the same idea also calls for care. More speed carries a grind farther, but it also means more energy to manage if the trick goes wrong. A safe plan adds a little speed at a time. If your grind keeps stopping halfway, a small increase in speed often fixes it, because a small change in speed makes a bigger change in distance.

words.d: a pattern where one amount grows with the square of another, so doubling one makes the other four times bigger
how fast something moves, in meters per second
the ability to do work; a moving board has energy that friction must use up to stop it

look.title: Grind Distance at Different Speeds
look.cite: Worked example with g = 9.8 m/s² and an example coefficient μ = 0.30
look.prompt: Compare the 1.0 m/s and 3.0 m/s rows. The speed tripled. About how many times farther did the board go?

check.q: If you double your speed onto a ledge, how much farther does the grind go?
check.why: Distance depends on v squared, and 2 squared is 4.

check.q: In the chart, how far does the board go at 4.0 m/s?
check.why: d = 16 divided by 5.88 = 2.72 m.

check.q: Your grind keeps stopping halfway. What small change does the reading suggest?
check.why: Because distance grows with speed squared, a little more speed carries the grind much farther.

lessons.title: Wax Halves the Mu
lessons.mainIdea: Lowering the coefficient of friction makes a grind go farther; halving μ doubles the slide distance.
reading: In the formula d = v squared divided by (2μg), μ sits on the bottom. When the bottom gets smaller, the answer gets bigger. Cut μ in half and the distance doubles. This is the pattern Deshawn and Ana measured: same speed, same ledge, but the waxed half let the trucks slide about twice as far.

Here is a worked example. Both skaters arrive at 3.0 m/s, so v squared = 9.0. On bare concrete, with an example μ = 0.40, the bottom is 2 times 0.40 times 9.8 = 7.84, so d = 9.0 divided by 7.84 = 1.15 m. On the waxed half, with an example μ = 0.20, the bottom is 2 times 0.20 times 9.8 = 3.92, so d = 9.0 divided by 3.92 = 2.30 m. Half the μ, twice the distance.

Wax lowers μ by putting a soft, slippery layer between the metal truck and the hard edge. The truck glides over the wax instead of catching on bumps in the concrete or paint. As skaters grind, the wax gets scraped away and pushed off the ends, so μ creeps back up. That is why the first grinds after waxing feel fast and later ones slow down.

words.d: a soft, slippery coating that lowers the coefficient of friction on an edge
the number μ that tells how strongly two surfaces resist sliding; smaller means slicker
a pattern where one amount gets bigger as another gets smaller

look.title: Slide Distance at 3 m/s for Different Surfaces
look.cite: Worked example with g = 9.8 m/s², v = 3.0 m/s and example coefficients
look.prompt: Find the rows for μ = 0.20 and μ = 0.40. How do their distances compare?

check.q: If wax cuts μ in half, what happens to the slide distance at the same speed?
choices: it becomes four times as long
check.why: μ is on the bottom of d = v²/(2μg), so halving μ doubles d.

check.q: In the worked example, how far does the board go on the waxed half?
check.why: d = 9.0 divided by 3.92 = 2.30 m.

check.q: Why do later grinds after waxing feel slower?
choices: the wax is scraped away, so μ creeps back up
check.why: Grinding wears off the wax, raising the friction again.

lessons.title: Metal, Concrete and Paint
lessons.mainIdea: Different edges have different friction: smooth metal is usually slick, bare concrete grabs, and paint changes as it wears.
reading: Skateparks build edges from a few materials, and each grinds differently. Many ledges have a *ledge cap*, a strip of steel angle iron along the top corner. Steel is smooth and hard, so trucks slide along it well, and the steel protects the concrete from chipping. Round steel rails and flat bars are also slick, especially after a little wax.

Bare concrete is rougher. Its surface has sand and small stones in it, which catch the trucks and raise the coefficient of friction. Fresh concrete can feel sticky until skaters wear it smooth and wax it. Concrete also crumbles at the corner over time, so a bare edge can get chipped, which makes the board hang up.

Paint changes over time. A newly painted curb can feel slick at first because the paint fills the rough pits in the concrete. As skaters grind it, the paint wears through in patches, and those bare spots grab. For example, a skater may feel the board slow suddenly when the trucks reach a chipped patch. Checking an edge with your hand before skating it is a smart habit.

words.d: a steel strip along the top corner of a ledge that protects it and helps boards slide
a long piece of steel bent into an L shape, often used as a ledge cap
a building material made of cement, sand and small stones that hardens like stone

look.title: Three Edges in a Row
look.text: Picture three low ledges side by side at a skatepark. The first has a shiny steel cap with a light coat of wax. The second is bare gray concrete with a slightly sandy feel. The third is a yellow painted curb, smooth in the middle but worn to bare concrete at one end. A skater grinds each at the same speed.
look.prompt: Rank the three edges from longest grind to shortest. Where on the painted curb might the board slow suddenly?

check.q: Why do many skatepark ledges have a steel cap?
choices: steel is smooth and protects the concrete from chipping
check.why: A steel cap slides well and keeps the corner from crumbling.

check.q: Why does bare concrete usually grab trucks more than steel?
choices: sand and small stones in its surface catch the trucks
check.why: Concrete's rough surface raises the coefficient of friction.

check.q: Why might a board slow suddenly on an old painted curb?
choices: the trucks hit a patch where paint has worn to bare concrete
check.why: Worn patches of bare concrete grab more than the painted parts.

lessons.title: Heat and Wear
lessons.mainIdea: Friction turns the board's motion energy into heat and wears away the metal, wood and wax it rubs.
reading: A moving board carries *kinetic energy*, the energy of motion, equal to one half times mass times speed squared: KE = ½mv². When friction stops a grind, that energy does not vanish. It turns into *heat* in the trucks and the edge, and a little into sound. That is the rough scraping noise of a grind. Rub your hands together fast and you feel the same effect.

Here is a worked example. A 60 kg skater starts a grind at 3.0 m/s. KE = 0.5 times 60 times 3.0 squared = 0.5 times 60 times 9.0 = 270 joules. A joule is the SI unit of energy. Friction does work equal to force times distance: 176.4 N times 1.53 m = about 270 joules. The two numbers match, because friction used up all the kinetic energy.

Friction also causes *wear*, the slow loss of material from rubbing. Trucks are usually made of aluminum, which is softer than steel, so grinding steel rails shaves tiny amounts off the hangers over time. Slides wear the wood under the nose, tail and middle of the deck. Wax wears off ledges. A worn deck can get thin or chipped, so checking your board for cracks is part of grinding safely.

words.d: the energy of motion; KE = ½mv²
energy that flows as warmth; friction turns motion energy into heat
the SI unit of energy, written J
the slow loss of material from surfaces that rub together

look.title: Where the Energy Goes
look.text: Picture a grind in slow motion. At the start, the 60 kg skater moves at 3.0 m/s and carries 270 joules of motion energy. Halfway along, the board has slowed, and some of that energy has warmed the hangers and the steel cap. At the end, the board has stopped. All 270 joules have become heat and a little sound.
look.prompt: Touch your truck right after a long grind session. What might you feel, and why?

check.q: What happens to a board's kinetic energy when friction stops a grind?
choices: it moves into the wax as mass
it turns into heat and sound
check.why: Friction changes motion energy into heat, with a little sound.

check.q: What is the kinetic energy of a 40 kg skater moving at 2.0 m/s?
check.why: KE = 0.5 times 40 times 2.0 squared = 0.5 times 40 times 4.0 = 80 J.

check.q: Why do aluminum hangers wear down on steel rails?
choices: aluminum is softer than steel, so rubbing shaves it away
check.why: The softer metal loses material when the two rub.

lessons.title: Will It Reach the End?
lessons.mainIdea: Comparing the slide distance to the ledge's length tells you whether a grind will make it to the end.
reading: A skater wants to 50-50 a ledge 2.0 m long. The ledge is waxed steel, with an example μ = 0.25. She arrives at 2.5 m/s. Will she reach the end? First, square the speed: 2.5 times 2.5 = 6.25. Next, find the bottom: 2 times 0.25 times 9.8 = 4.9. Then divide: d = 6.25 divided by 4.9 = 1.28 m. That is short of 2.0 m, so the board stops about 0.7 m before the end.

What speed would carry her all the way? Use the formula backward: v squared = 2μgd = 2 times 0.25 times 9.8 times 2.0 = 9.8. The square root of 9.8 is about 3.13. She needs about 3.1 m/s as she starts the grind. That is only about 0.6 m/s more than before, yet it carries her 0.7 m farther.

She has two choices. She can bring a little more speed, or she can lower μ with fresh wax. If wax brings μ down to 0.20, then at 2.5 m/s the bottom becomes 2 times 0.20 times 9.8 = 3.92, and d = 6.25 divided by 3.92 = 1.59 m. Wax helps, but here it is not quite enough on its own. A small speed increase is the stronger fix.

words.d: a problem solved step by step to show how a method works
the number that, multiplied by itself, gives a certain value; the square root of 9 is 3
to rearrange a formula to find a starting value, such as the speed needed for a distance

check.q: At 2.5 m/s with μ = 0.25, how far does the board grind?
check.why: d = 6.25 divided by 4.9 = about 1.28 m.

check.q: About what speed is needed to grind the full 2.0 m with μ = 0.25?
check.why: v squared = 2 times 0.25 times 9.8 times 2.0 = 9.8, and the square root is about 3.1.

check.q: In this example, which fix helps more on its own?
check.why: Wax raises the grind to 1.59 m, but about 3.1 m/s carries the board the full 2.0 m.

lessons.title: Where the Model Stops
lessons.mainIdea: The formula is a good first model, but real grinds also depend on landing, slope, balance and changing friction.
reading: Every physics formula is a *model*, a simplified picture that matches reality in some ways. The formula d = v squared divided by (2μg) assumes a level edge, a steady μ and a board that slides the whole way. Real grinds break those rules in small ways. Knowing where a model stops helps you use it well.

Landing on the edge is one example. When the trucks hit the ledge after an ollie, the normal force spikes above the skater's weight for a split second. Friction spikes with it, so the board loses extra speed right at the start. Balance is another. If the skater leans and the board tips, the grind ends early, no matter what the formula says.

Slope changes the math too. On a gently sloped flat bar at a skatepark, gravity pulls the board along the slope and partly cancels friction, so the board slows less. On a sloped edge going up, gravity adds to the slowing. The coefficient also changes along a real edge as wax thins and paint wears. Even so, the main ideas hold: more speed and less friction mean a longer grind.

words.d: a simplified picture or formula that matches how something works in some ways
a surface that tilts up or down instead of being level
something a model takes as true to keep the math simple

look.title: Formula Versus Ledge
look.text: Picture a skater who calculated that her grind should go 1.5 m. She tries it and goes 1.2 m. On the next try, she lands softly with bent knees and goes 1.4 m. On a fresh coat of wax, she goes 1.8 m. Each change in the real world moved the result away from or toward the model.
look.prompt: Name two reasons a real grind might come up shorter than the formula predicts.

check.q: What is a model in physics?
choices: a simplified picture that matches reality in some ways
check.why: A model simplifies the real situation to make it easier to predict.

check.q: Why does a board lose extra speed when the trucks first land on the ledge?
choices: the normal force spikes, so friction spikes too
check.why: A hard landing pushes harder on the edge for a moment, raising f = μN.

check.q: Which assumption does d = v²/(2μg) make?
check.why: The formula comes from a = μg, which is true on a level edge.

review.q: Which way does kinetic friction push on a grinding board?
A skater and board have a mass of 70 kg. What is the normal force on a level ledge?
With N = 686 N and μ = 0.20, what is the friction force?
On a level ledge, the slowing of a grind is a = μg. What happened to mass?
review.why: a = μmg divided by m, so mass cancels.

review.q: With μ = 0.40, what is the slowing?
A board starts a grind at 3.0 m/s with μ = 0.30. How far does it go?
Which change makes a grind go four times as far?
review.why: Distance depends on v squared, so doubling v gives 4 times the distance.

review.q: Where does the board's kinetic energy go during a grind?
choices: into the wheels as more speed
review.why: Friction turns motion energy into heat and a little sound.
